URETHRAL DISCHARGE IN MEN (most commonly gonorrhoea or chlamydia): Symptoms include discharge from penis, pain on urination. Treatment: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose PLUS Azithromycin 1g orally single dose OR Doxycycline 100mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Treat partner. For vaginitis: Candidiasis - Clotrimazole pessary 500mg single dose OR Fluconazole 150mg orally single dose. Bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis - Metronidazole 2g orally single dose OR 400mg twice daily for 7 days. GENITAL ULCER DISEASE (may be syphilis, chancroid, or herpes): Treatment: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM single dose PLUS Azithromycin 1g orally single dose OR Erythromycin 500mg orally 4 times daily for 7 days. If herpes suspected, add Acyclovir 400mg orally 3 times daily for 7 days. PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE (PID): Lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, fever, cervical motion tenderness. Treatment: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose PLUS Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 14 days PLUS Metronidazole 400mg twice daily for 14 days.

passage: Chlamydial Infection: C. trachomatis immunotypes D-K are isolated in about 50% of cases of non-gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis. Clinical Features: Often asymptomatic, incubation period usually 10-20 days. Co-infection with gonococci and chlamydiae is common. Urethral or cervical discharge tends to be less painful, less purulent, and watery compared with gonococcal infection. Complications: Epididymo-orchitis and sterility in males, Pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility in females, Adverse pregnancy outcomes, Conjunctivitis and pneumonia in the newborn. Drug Treatment — Recommended regimen: Doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days. Or Azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose. Chlamydial infection during pregnancy: Erythromycin 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days. Or Amoxycillin 500 mg orally every 8 hours for 7 days. Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis (incubation 10-14 days compared to 2-3 days for gonococcal): Erythromycin syrup 50 mg/kg per day orally every 6 hours for 14 days. Or Trimethoprim 40 mg with sulfamethoxazole 200 mg orally every 12 hours for 14 days. No evidence that additional topical agent provides further benefit. If inclusion conjunctivitis recurs after therapy, reinstitute erythromycin for 2 weeks. Important to treat the mother and her sexual partner. Doxycycline/tetracycline: should not be given to children under 12 years, or to pregnant or breastfeeding women due to deposition in growing bones and teeth.

passage: Peripheral Vascular Disease: A chronic and progressive disease due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the peripheral blood vessels. Commonly affects the peripheral arteries of the legs. Other peripheral vessels that may be affected are that of stomach, arms or head. Clinical Features: Hair loss on the feet and legs and brittle toenails, intermittent claudication, numbness in the legs, sores or ulcers on the legs and feet that take a long time to heal, difficulty in finding a pulse in the leg or foot, erectile dysfunction. Differential Diagnoses: Deep venous thrombosis (DVT), lumbar (intervertebral) disk disorders, mechanical back pain, septic thrombophlebitis, superficial thrombophlebitis. Complications: Amputation, poor wound healing, restricted mobility due to pain or discomfort, severe pain in the affected extremity, stroke. Investigations: Ankle Brachial Index (ABI), a pulse volume record, a vascular ultrasound.

passage: MALE CONDOM: A rubber (latex) sheath worn on an erect penis before and during sexual intercourse. How it works: Prevents sperm from entering the vagina by collecting ejaculate. Also provides barrier protection against STIs including HIV. Effectiveness: 98% effective with perfect use, 82% with typical use. Advantages: Only method that protects against both pregnancy AND STIs/HIV (dual protection). No hormonal side effects. Available without prescription. Can be used as backup method. Male involvement in family planning. Disadvantages: Must be used correctly with every act of intercourse. May reduce sensation. Requires partner cooperation. May interrupt sex to put on. Can break or slip off if not used correctly. Correct use: Use new condom for each act of intercourse. Check expiry date. Open package carefully - do not use teeth or sharp objects. Pinch tip of condom to remove air. Unroll condom all the way down erect penis before any genital contact. After ejaculation, hold base of condom while withdrawing. Remove carefully and dispose. Do not reuse.

passage: Peripheral Vascular Disease: A chronic and progressive disease due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the peripheral blood vessels. Commonly affects the peripheral arteries of the legs. Other peripheral vessels that may be affected are that of stomach, arms or head. Clinical Features: Hair loss on the feet and legs and brittle toenails, intermittent claudication, numbness in the legs, sores or ulcers on the legs and feet that take a long time to heal, difficulty in finding a pulse in the leg or foot, erectile dysfunction. Differential Diagnoses: Deep venous thrombosis (DVT), lumbar (intervertebral) disk disorders, mechanical back pain, septic thrombophlebitis, superficial thrombophlebitis. Complications: Amputation, poor wound healing, restricted mobility due to pain or discomfort, severe pain in the affected extremity, stroke. Investigations: Ankle Brachial Index (ABI), a pulse volume record, a vascular ultrasound.

passage: MALE CONDOM: A rubber (latex) sheath worn on an erect penis before and during sexual intercourse. How it works: Prevents sperm from entering the vagina by collecting ejaculate. Also provides barrier protection against STIs including HIV. Effectiveness: 98% effective with perfect use, 82% with typical use. Advantages: Only method that protects against both pregnancy AND STIs/HIV (dual protection). No hormonal side effects. Available without prescription. Can be used as backup method. Male involvement in family planning. Disadvantages: Must be used correctly with every act of intercourse. May reduce sensation. Requires partner cooperation. May interrupt sex to put on. Can break or slip off if not used correctly. Correct use: Use new condom for each act of intercourse. Check expiry date. Open package carefully - do not use teeth or sharp objects. Pinch tip of condom to remove air. Unroll condom all the way down erect penis before any genital contact. After ejaculation, hold base of condom while withdrawing. Remove carefully and dispose. Do not reuse.
